title: The Four Skills in Practice

points.sub: Two kinds of processing at once
pts: Bottom-up processing decodes sounds, words and grammar; top-down processing uses context and prior knowledge to predict meaning.
Weak listeners often over-rely on one mode — pre-listening tasks activate top-down prediction before the audio even starts.
Train both explicitly rather than assuming comprehension will follow from exposure alone.
points.who: John Field, "Listening in the Language Classroom"

v: Ten sentences for the teacher to say at natural speed

items: Tell learners you will say a sentence once, at normal speed. They write only the number of words they hear.
Say the first sentence: What do you want to do? Learners write a number.
Reveal the answer (6). Say the sentence again slowly, then naturally, and ask where the words ‘disappeared’ (d’you, wanna).
Repeat with the other sentences. After each one, learners compare answers with a partner before you reveal.
Finish with a top-down contrast: say only the title of a story (The Lost Ticket) and ask learners to predict three words they will hear.
Learners write the whole sentence after counting (a short dictation).
Use sentences from the next listening text, so the practice prepares learners for it.
Support: say each sentence twice.
Stretch: include sentences with contractions and linking (I’d’ve gone).

lines: Where’s he gone? (3) / I don’t know. (3) / Can I have a cup of tea? (7) / It’s a lot of work. (5) / What are you going to do? (6)

blocks.x: Why it matters: many learners know every word in What are you going to do? but cannot recognize it as /wɒtʃə ˈɡʌnə duː/ in fast speech. That is a bottom-up problem, and no amount of prediction solves it.

body: Purpose: to explain bottom-up and top-down processing. Content: a vertical diagram. At the bottom, a sound wave labelled ‘sounds → words → sentences’ with an upward arrow (‘bottom-up’). At the top, a thought cloud labelled ‘topic, situation, what I already know’ with a downward arrow (‘top-down’). The arrows meet in the middle at a box labelled ‘meaning’. Style: two colours, one per direction. Board version: two arrows meeting in a box.

items: ELLLO (English Listening Lesson Library Online; free). Short recordings by speakers from many countries, with transcripts. Choose a clip, take two sentences from the transcript and use them for counting.

blocks.x: Your own voice is the ideal source: you can adjust speed instantly. Keep a notebook of useful sentences for counting.

body: In fast speech, the words of English run together so completely that a sentence can contain no pauses between words at all. Listeners separate them using their knowledge of the language. Learners are not failing to hear pauses; the pauses are not there.

pts: Pre-listening: activate schema and pre-teach only the vocabulary that blocks comprehension.
While-listening: set a different, narrower task for each replay — gist first, detail second.
Post-listening: move from comprehension into production, using the audio as a model.
points.who: Penny Ur, "A Course in Language Teaching"

v: The script below (read by the teacher or recorded); a simple train timetable on the board

items: Pre-listening. Show a picture of a busy railway platform. Ask: ‘What do you hear at a station?’ Collect ideas in any language, then in English.
Pre-teach only the words that would block understanding: platform, delayed, depart.
First listening (gist). ‘Is the news good or bad for passengers?’
Second listening (detail). Learners complete the timetable: train number, destination, new platform, new time.
Third listening (language). Learners listen for the phrase that means ‘we are sorry’ (We regret the inconvenience).
Post-listening. In pairs, learners write and perform their own announcement for a different train, using the model.
Use a school assembly announcement or a local radio weather report.
Record learners’ announcements and play them as a listening task for another class.
Support: give a partly completed timetable.
Stretch: learners listen for, and explain, the difference between delayed and cancelled.

lines: Attention please. Train number one-two-six-two-seven, the Chennai Express, is delayed by twenty-five minutes. It will now depart at ten-fifteen from platform number four, not platform number two. We regret the inconvenience caused to passengers.

blocks.x: The listening task for each hearing:

lines: 1st: gist (good or bad news?) / 2nd: details (timetable) / 3rd: language (a useful phrase)

body: Purpose: to model staged listening. Content: three ear icons in a row, numbered 1–3. Under each, a task label and a small symbol: a thumbs up/down (‘gist’), a table (‘detail’), a speech bubble with words (‘language’). Above the row, a small box labelled ‘Before: predict + key words’; after the row, a box labelled ‘After: use it’. Style: simple, horizontal flow. Board version: 1–2–3 with task words.

items: Vocaroo (free). Record the announcement once in your own voice so the three hearings are identical; learners can also record their own announcements in step 6.

blocks.x: Read the script aloud each time at the same speed. For the third hearing, slow down slightly on the target phrase.

body: Set a different task for each hearing. ‘Listen again’ with the same questions tells learners they failed the first time. A new, narrower task tells them what to listen for.

pts: Controlled practice narrows the target language to build accuracy under low communicative pressure.
Fluency tasks widen the language allowed but demand real, unscripted communication.
Mixing the two in one activity confuses the learner about which goal they're being judged on.

v: A timer; a list of topics

items: Learners choose a topic they know well (my best friend, my village, a festival, a film).
Give two minutes of silent planning: notes only, no full sentences.
Pair learners. Speaker A talks about the topic for four minutes while B listens.
A moves to a new partner and gives the same talk in three minutes; then to a third partner in two minutes.
Swap roles and repeat.
Ask speakers: ‘What changed between the first and the third talk?’ Most notice they spoke faster and hesitated less.
In a separate, later stage, give a short controlled accuracy task on one error you noticed (for example, past tense forms).
In a fixed-bench classroom, use 3/2/1 minutes and rotate by turning to the person in front, beside and behind.
For young learners, 2/1.5/1 minutes with picture prompts.
Support: allow a card with five key words during the first talk only.
Stretch: the listener must ask one question at the end of each talk.

blocks.x: Accuracy and fluency activities side by side:

lines: Accuracy: Repeat and change: I went to the market. → She… → They… → Yesterday we… (narrow language, correction expected)
Fluency: Tell your partner about the best day of your holiday. (open language, no interruption)
S2: Really? What happened next?
S2: That sounds great. Who was with you?

body: Purpose: to show the rotation clearly. Content: three pairs of chairs arranged in a line. Arrows show speaker A moving from pair 1 to pair 2 to pair 3. Above each pair, a clock face showing 4, 3 and 2 minutes. A small graph beside it shows ‘pauses’ decreasing and ‘speed’ increasing across the three talks. Style: plan view, clean icons. Board version: three boxes with 4 → 3 → 2.

items: Online Stopwatch or Classroomscreen (free). A large, visible countdown keeps the rotations fair.

blocks.x: A phone timer or wristwatch and a clear signal (a clap or bell) to change partners.

points.sub: Language with a real reason to exist
pts: A genuine information gap — one learner has data the other needs — forces authentic negotiation of meaning.
Contrast with display questions, where the teacher already knows the answer and learners perform rather than communicate.
Interaction that requires negotiation of meaning is where acquisition is argued to happen.

v: Pairs of pictures (A and B) of a market scene with eight differences (see Appendix)

items: Pair learners and give A and B their pictures. They must not show them to each other.
Pre-teach or elicit the language for describing position (next to, behind, on the left).
Learners describe their pictures and ask questions to find eight differences.
When they think they have them all, they compare pictures and check.
Feedback: which questions were most useful? Write them on the board.
Replace pictures with two versions of a school timetable or a bus route.
In a larger ‘jigsaw’ version, four learners each hold one quarter of a map.
Support: provide a list of objects in the picture.
Stretch: learners must find the differences without saying the names of the objects (the round, red fruit…).

blocks.x: A genuine gap versus a display question:

lines: Display: T: What colour is the bag? (the teacher can see it)
Genuine: S1: In my picture there are three bananas. How many in yours? (only S2 knows)

blocks.x: Negotiating meaning when it breaks down:

lines: S1: There is a man with a… thela… a cart, on the left.
S2: A cart? With fruit?
S1: No, with vegetables.

body: Figure 3.4 Market scene, pictures A and B

Purpose: photocopiable information-gap task. Content: two nearly identical line drawings of an Indian street market: vegetable carts, a fruit stall, a tea stall, a cow, a scooter, a woman with a shopping bag, a boy with a kite, a signboard. Eight clear differences (number of bananas; cow present/absent; signboard text; kite colour; scooter position; teapot on/off stove; bag colour; a dog under the cart). Style: black and white line art, uncluttered, printable A4 landscape. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Slides (free). Put picture A and picture B on separate slides shared with different learners, so each can see only one on a phone.

blocks.x: Paper pictures, as in the activity. For a class of sixty, prepare fifteen copies of each picture for groups of four (two As and two Bs).

pts: Intensive reading works a short text hard for detail, structure and language analysis.
Extensive reading moves through long, easy texts (roughly one level below current ability) for fluency and enjoyment.
Most syllabuses over-invest in intensive reading and starve the extensive reading that builds real fluency.
points.who: Richard Day & Julian Bamford, "Extensive Reading in the Second Language Classroom"

blocks.x: A class library and a reading log

v: 10 minutes per lesson for extensive reading; 30 minutes for the intensive task
A box of easy books or printed stories at several levels; reading logs

items: Extensive. Set up a class library: graded readers, children’s books, printed stories, magazines in English. Aim for books slightly below learners’ level.
Explain the rules: choose any book; stop reading if you don’t like it; no tests.
Give ten minutes of silent reading at the start of two lessons a week. Read yourself at the same time.
Learners record title, pages and one reaction word in a reading log.
Intensive. Once a week, take a short text (150 words) and work on it closely: meaning, language, structure.
Compare: ‘Which reading was easier? Which taught you more new words? Which did you enjoy?’
Parallel texts: provide a few stories in both English and a home language, so learners can read one and check the other.
Learners write short recommendations on a ‘Books we liked’ chart.
Support: start with picture books and very short stories.
Stretch: learners read a longer book and give a two-minute book talk.

lines: Extensive: long, easy, chosen by the learner, for pleasure and fluency, no test.
Intensive: short, challenging, chosen by the teacher, for detail and language study.
Title: The Monkey and the Crocodile. Pages: 12. Word: funny.

body: Purpose: to contrast extensive and intensive reading. Content: a split image. Left: a child lying comfortably on a mat with a stack of thin books, a speech bubble ‘easy, lots, for fun’. Right: the same child at a desk with one page, a pencil and a magnifying glass, a bubble ‘short, hard, look closely’. Style: warm, friendly illustration. Board version: two lists under the headings ‘lots and easy’ and ‘little and hard’.

items: StoryWeaver (free, by Pratham Books). A large library of openly licensed children’s stories in English and many Indian languages, graded by reading level. Stories can be read online or downloaded and printed. [VERIFY current number of titles and languages before stating figures.]
Global Storybooks (free). Openly licensed stories available in multiple languages with audio for some titles.

blocks.x: Collect stories from old textbooks, newspapers and children’s magazines; print StoryWeaver stories once and laminate them. A shoebox library of fifty short texts can serve a whole school year.

pts: Skimming for gist, scanning for specific information, and inferring meaning from context are distinct, teachable skills.
Predicting from titles, headings and images primes comprehension before the first line is read.
Test reading sub-skills separately — a single comprehension quiz conflates several different abilities.
points.who: Christine Nuttall, "Teaching Reading Skills in a Foreign Language"

v: A bus timetable, a TV schedule or a school notice (one copy per pair)

items: Show only the title and headings of the text. Learners predict what it will tell them (predicting).
Give 30 seconds for learners to skim the whole text and say what kind of text it is and what it is for (skimming).
Scan race: call out a question (What time is the last bus to Mysuru?). The first pair to point to the answer wins a point (scanning).
Ask one inference question: Why do you think there are more buses on Sunday? (inferring).
Ask learners which sub-skill each stage practised.
Use a menu, a cricket scorecard or a cinema listing.
Learners write scan questions for another pair.
Support: highlight the column where the answers are.
Stretch: include questions whose answer is not in the text, so learners must say ‘It doesn’t say’.

lines: Predict: It’s a bus timetable, so I expect times and places.
Skim: It shows buses from Bengaluru to three cities.
Scan: The last bus to Mysuru is at 22:30.
Infer: More people travel on Sunday, maybe to visit family.

body: Purpose: to contrast skimming and scanning. Content: two identical small pages of text. On the first, a smooth zigzag line from top to bottom (‘skim: the whole page, quickly’). On the second, a straight line that jumps directly to one highlighted number (‘scan: find one thing’). Style: minimal, one accent colour. Board version: two rectangles with a zigzag and an arrow.

items: Wordwall (free basic version). Create a ‘Find the match’ or ‘Quiz’ activity with scanning questions projected for a team race.

blocks.x: Photocopy a real local timetable or copy one onto the board. Real documents motivate more than invented ones.

pts: Plan, draft, revise and edit are recursive stages, not one linear pass from blank page to final copy.
Peer feedback between drafts teaches revision as a skill, not just correction as a punishment.
Separate content and organisation feedback from surface-level grammar and punctuation feedback.
points.who: Process-writing approach; Ann Raimes, "Techniques in Teaching Writing"

v: A model email; a peer checklist

items: Plan. Learners are going to write an email inviting a friend to a festival at their home. Brainstorm ideas in a quick mind map.
Draft. Learners write a first draft in 10 minutes. Tell them not to worry about spelling yet.
Share. Learners swap drafts with a partner, who uses the checklist to comment on content and organization only.
Revise. Learners rewrite, using their partner’s comments.
Edit. In the next lesson, learners check grammar, spelling and punctuation, using a short editing list.
Publish. Display the final emails, or send them to a partner class.
Write the first draft in pairs.
Use a real purpose: a thank-you letter to a visitor, a notice for the school board.
Support: give a model email with some parts missing.
Stretch: learners write a reply to their partner’s email.

lines: Does it say what the festival is? When and where? Is there a friendly opening and ending? Is there one thing you want to know more about?

blocks.x: Two kinds of feedback, kept apart:

lines: Content: I want to know what food there will be!
Language (later): festivel → festival.

body: Purpose: to show that writing is recursive. Content: a circle of five stages (plan, draft, share, revise, edit) with a separate arrow to ‘publish’. Smaller curved arrows show movement backwards (revise → draft, edit → revise). Style: clean cycle diagram. Board version: five words in a circle with arrows.

items: Google Docs (free). Learners share drafts; partners use ‘Comment’ for content feedback. ‘Version history’ shows how the text changed between drafts.
Write & Improve (by Cambridge; free with registration). Learners submit a draft and receive automatic feedback on language; best used at the editing stage, not for content.

blocks.x: Write on alternate lines so there is space for changes. Use a pencil for drafts and pen for final versions.

body: Collect first and final drafts from five learners. Count the changes that concern ideas and organization and the changes that concern spelling and grammar. If almost all the changes are small corrections, your learners may be editing but not yet revising.

pts: A single topic can carry learners from listening input, into discussion, into extension reading, into a written response.
Integration mirrors real language use, where skills rarely operate alone.
Plan the arc backwards from the final output task to keep every stage purposeful.
points.who: Jack C. Richards, "Communicative Language Teaching Today"

v: A short listening text, a short reading text and a writing task on the same topic

items: Plan backwards. Decide the final task first: each learner writes an invitation to a festival. Then decide what learners need to hear, say and read to do it well.
Listening. The teacher describes her favourite festival (two minutes). Learners note what, when, food, clothes.
Speaking. In groups, learners tell each other about a festival they celebrate.
Reading. Learners read a short blog post about a festival in another country and find three new words.
Writing. Learners write their invitation, using ideas and words from the earlier stages.
Reflect. Which stage helped most with the writing?
Change the topic to a match, a wedding, a science fair or a school trip.
Replace step 4 with a short video if devices are available.
Support: provide a writing frame for the invitation.
Stretch: learners add a short paragraph comparing two festivals.

lines: Final task: invitation (writing) ← needs: dates, food, activities vocabulary; friendly tone ← reading: model of describing a festival ← speaking: rehearse ideas aloud ← listening: first exposure to language.
Dear ______, I am writing to invite you to ______. It is on ______. We will ______. Please come!

body: Purpose: to show planning from the final task. Content: a horizontal arrow pointing left from a box labelled ‘Final task’ to three boxes labelled ‘What must they read?’, ‘What must they say?’, ‘What must they hear?’. Beneath, a second arrow pointing right labelled ‘Teaching order’. Style: two-tone arrows. Board version: as described.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers). Learners design their invitations as simple posters, which adds a real audience and purpose.

blocks.x: Invitations on folded card, decorated by hand and displayed on a class wall.

dek: Unit 3 of 100: Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing are never taught in isolation — this poster stages each skill and shows how one topic can move learners through all four in a single lesson.

aims.x: This unit moves from naming the four skills to teaching them. It gives each skill a clear lesson shape and ends by showing how a single topic can carry learners through all four in one lesson.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain bottom-up and top-down listening and train both;
stage a listening lesson in three phases with a different task for each hearing;
plan speaking activities that aim clearly at either accuracy or fluency;
design information-gap tasks that require real communication;
distinguish extensive from intensive reading and make room for both;
teach reading sub-skills separately and in combination;
run writing as a process of drafting and revising;
plan an integrated-skills lesson backwards from its final task.

why: Why this matters. Unit 1 named the four skills as one of eight foundations. A skill named but not staged stays abstract — this poster gives each one a teachable sequence.

background.x: The four skills are a tidy way of describing something untidy. In real life, people rarely use one skill on its own. A railway passenger listens to an announcement, reads the departure board, asks a stranger and writes a quick message home, all within two minutes. Teaching skills separately is useful because each has its own difficulties; teaching them together is necessary because that is how they are used.

Each skill is itself a bundle of processes. Listening, for instance, involves recognizing sounds and words as they rush past (what researchers call bottom-up processing) and at the same time using what we already know about the topic and the situation to predict and interpret (top-down processing). John Field (2008) argues that many listening lessons test comprehension rather than teach it: learners hear a recording, answer questions and find out whether they were right, without ever being shown how to listen better. The same criticism can be made of many reading and writing lessons.

This unit therefore treats each skill as something to be taught, not only practised. For each one, it offers a lesson shape that includes preparation, a clear task and a follow-up that turns comprehension or production into learning. In multilingual classrooms, there is a further resource: learners who read, listen and write in other languages already have many of these processes. A learner who predicts the ending of a Kannada story can predict the ending of an English one, if the teacher invites her to.

items: Listening progress. Repeat the word-counting activity with new sentences each month and record average accuracy.
Speaking fluency. Time one learner’s first and third 4/3/2 talks; count pauses per minute. Repeat after four weeks.
Reading log review. Count pages read per learner per month; talk to learners who read very little.
Writing drafts. Assess the final email with a short rubric covering content, organization and language, and compare first and final drafts.
When did you last teach listening, rather than test it?
Which of your speaking activities are clearly aimed at accuracy, and which at fluency? Do learners know which is which?
How much reading do your learners do in a week? Could ten minutes of free reading fit into your timetable?
Do you mark first drafts? What would change if you gave only content feedback on them?
Think of a topic you taught recently. What would it look like if you planned it backwards from a final task?

perm: The platform announcement, market pictures and festival texts are original. StoryWeaver and Global Storybooks content is openly licensed; check the specific licence of any story reproduced. Screenshots of ELLLO, Wordwall, Google Docs, Write & Improve or Canva require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: A fluency activity in which a learner gives the same talk three times to different listeners in four, three and then two minutes, so that repetition and time pressure make speech smoother (Nation 1989).

The extent to which a learner’s language is free from errors in grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation; one of the three dimensions of performance, with complexity and fluency, that teachers balance in task design.
Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
Understanding a text by building meaning from its smallest parts, such as sounds, letters, words and grammar; it complements top-down processing, which uses background knowledge and expectations.

A question to which the teacher already knows the answer, asked to check knowledge or display language, such as ‘What’s the capital of Karnataka?’ It contrasts with a genuine question (Long and Sato 1983).
The final stage of process writing, in which learners check and correct grammar, spelling and punctuation after the content and organization have been revised, often using a short editing checklist.

Reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, such as graded readers or StoryWeaver books (Day and Bamford 1998). It builds fluency, vocabulary and reading habits.
The ability to speak or write at a natural speed with limited hesitation, focusing on meaning. It is often balanced against accuracy and complexity in planning tasks and giving feedback.
The general meaning or main idea of a text. Reading or listening for gist means getting an overall understanding without attending to every detail, often as a first task.
A book written or adapted for language learners within a controlled range of vocabulary and grammar, used for extensive reading at the right level.
Working out meaning that is not directly stated in a text, using clues and background knowledge, such as a character’s feelings or a writer’s attitude.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.
Teaching listening, speaking, reading and writing together, as they are used in real life, rather than as separate subjects, for example reading an article and then discussing and writing about it.
Close, detailed reading of a short text, often with attention to vocabulary, grammar and meaning, as distinct from extensive reading for pleasure.
An approach to teaching writing that focuses on the stages writers go through, such as planning, drafting, revising and editing, with feedback from teacher or peers between drafts.

In process writing, making changes to the content, ideas and organization of a draft, as distinct from editing, which corrects spelling, grammar and punctuation. Learners often edit but do not yet revise.
Reading quickly to find specific information, such as a date, name or figure, without reading the whole text. Looking up a train time in a timetable is a typical scanning task.
Reading quickly to get the general idea or gist of a text, without attending to detail, for example glancing through a newspaper article to see what it is about before deciding whether to read it.
Understanding a text by drawing on background knowledge, context and expectations about the topic and genre, rather than decoding word by word. It works together with bottom-up processing.
